issues.explanation: Fire/flames is not a plausible primary trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver unless other profile elements indicate fire-related abuse or a fire context, which they do not. The rest of the trigger, threat, memory, and appraisal items point to interpersonal threat rather than burn/fire trauma, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: Survival guilt about others dying is difficult to reconcile with childhood physical abuse by a caregiver when no other items reference deaths, fatalities, or witnessing others die. It also conflicts with the rest of the profile, which centers on helplessness and failure to stop abuse rather than surviving when others did not.

vignette:
Margaret, a 73-year-old QA engineer, still carries the weight of a childhood she rarely speaks about. When she was eight, her father-the man she trusted most-would punish her for small mistakes with unpredictable beatings. She remembers one afternoon in particular with photographic clarity: the way the light fell across the kitchen linoleum, the pattern on his shirt, the exact sound of his belt buckle. Even now, recalling that scene, she sometimes feels completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, and she can never find the right words to describe what she endured. What has stayed with her most sharply is a sense of betrayal-she was supposed to be safe with him-and a crushing helplessness that she can't stop bad things from happening to her, along with a guilt she will never forgive herself for: not doing more to stop what happened.

Those appraisals have shaped how she moves through the world. Uncertainty of any kind-an ambiguous email from a male colleague, an unmarked change in software requirements-floods her with hypervigilance. Her body reacts before her mind can catch up: heart pounding, breath shallow, as though danger is already upon her. Sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard, and being alone with men triggers an automatic, visceral alarm. She has come to believe that every ambiguous situation, every male presence, every reminder of death-she avoids funerals and cemeteries entirely-is a threat waiting to unfold. A few months ago, a coworker invited her to his mother's funeral; she declined without explanation, but the mere invitation brought back the memory of her father's funeral at age fifteen, and with it the old helplessness and guilt.

Her beliefs about herself reinforce the way she recalls the abuse. Because she sees herself as someone who failed to act, her memory of the beatings often surfaces not as a story she can narrate but as a series of sharp, silent images-photographs in her mind-that she cannot translate into words. When she is alone with a male colleague in a conference room, her negative appraisals intensify: she becomes hypervigilant, certain that she is vulnerable again, and this threat state confirms her belief that she is inherently helpless. She thinks, "I can't stop this from happening," even when nothing is happening. That conviction, in turn, makes her scan the environment for signs of danger, so that even ordinary male presence becomes a perceived trigger.

At work, she has learned to avoid situations that involve unpredictability, delegating tasks that require spontaneous meetings with male team members. She stays in her cubicle, running regression tests in silence. The hypervigilance and bodily reactions she experiences around male coworkers only deepen her sense that she is still the powerless child she was sixty-five years ago. She has never told her husband the full story; she fears he would see her as broken. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at a funeral visitation for a distant relative-she had felt compelled to go, but the sight of the casket triggered a photographic memory so vivid she excused herself, trembling, and drove home in a state of panic. Now she is afraid that she will never be able to feel safe again, and she is desperate to understand why a lifetime of avoidance has not protected her from the past.
